migrationNotes: Spine: Follow one ball from the throw to the catch: what it carries (momentum), how a push over time removes it (impulse), how that gives a final velocity, and why a longer stop means a smaller force.
Left out of the lesson (still in the course): phys-momentum-and-impulse-6.

lesson.title: Momentum and impulse

lead.text: Think about stopping two things that move at the same speed, a tennis ball and a bowling ball, both rolling towards you at walking pace. The tennis ball is easy to stop and the bowling ball is hard. Take one bowling ball and roll it faster and it becomes harder again. How hard something is to stop depends on its mass and on its velocity.

Physicists multiply the two together and call the result momentum. Momentum = mass × velocity, written p = mv, and its unit is the kilogram metre per second (kg·m/s). A 1 kg ball moving at 5 m/s has a momentum of 5 kg·m/s. A 10 kg bowling ball at the same velocity has 50 kg·m/s.

Velocity has a direction, so momentum has a direction too. It takes its sign from the velocity. With right taken as positive, a 1 kg ball moving left at 7 m/s has a momentum of −7 kg·m/s. Kinetic energy has no direction, because it depends on the speed squared.
Take right as positive and use the sign of the velocity.

reveal.text: You multiplied the mass by the signed velocity, and rightward motion gives a positive result.

steps.headline: A push that lasts for a time

lead.text: Momentum changes when something pushes. Push a stationary trolley with a steady force and it starts to move. Keep pushing and it moves faster. Two things decide how much momentum you give it: how hard you push and how long you keep pushing. A strong push that lasts a split second can give the same as a gentle push that lasts a long time.

The force multiplied by the time it acts for is called impulse. Impulse = F × Δt, where Δt means the time the force acts for. Its unit is the newton second (N·s) and it takes its sign from the force. An impulse equals the change in momentum that it produces. That change is written Δp and is the final momentum minus the initial momentum.

afterFigure.text: Suppose a steady 10 N push acts on a 5 kg trolley for 3 s. The impulse is 10 × 3 = 30 N·s, so a trolley that started at rest ends with 30 kg·m/s. The figure shows that push lasting 3 s and then 1 s. The longer push gives three times the impulse, so it leaves the trolley with three times the momentum. In every case the force here is the net force, the total of everything pushing on the trolley.

lead.text: Use the size of the force and how long it lasts.

steps.headline: From a push to a final velocity

lead.text: Because impulse equals the change in momentum, final momentum = initial momentum + impulse. Take a 4 kg cart rolling right at 1 m/s. Its momentum is 4 × 1 = 4 kg·m/s. A net impulse of +12 N·s takes that to 16 kg·m/s. Momentum is mass times velocity, so divide by the mass: 16 ÷ 4 = 4 m/s.

The sign of the impulse matters, because an impulse that points against the motion takes momentum away. An impulse of −4 N·s brings the same cart's momentum to zero and stops it. A larger impulse of −12 N·s turns it round, since 4 − 12 = −8 kg·m/s, which is 2 m/s to the left.
To find a final velocity, start from the initial momentum and add the impulse with its sign. Then divide by the mass. The next screen works through this on a pushed cart.

steps.headline: A 2 kg cart moves at +3 m/s. A 5 N net force acts for 4 s. Find its final velocity.

workedSteps.text: Impulse is force times time. Add it to the momentum.

steps.headline: A 3 kg cart moves at +4 m/s. A net impulse of +18 N·s acts. Find its final velocity.
Why a longer stop is gentler

lead.text: Back to the ball. Catching it brings its momentum to zero, so the impulse needed depends only on how much momentum it has. A 2 kg ball moving at 5 m/s carries 10 kg·m/s, so catching it takes an impulse of −10 N·s whatever your hands do.

Impulse is force times time, so the force is the impulse divided by the time: F = Δp ÷ Δt. This is the average net force during the stop. Stop the ball in 0.5 s and the average force is −10 ÷ 0.5 = −20 N. Stop it in 2 s and the average force is −10 ÷ 2 = −5 N. The minus sign says the force points against the motion.

afterFigure.text: Both cases in the figure remove the same momentum, but the longer stop needs a quarter of the force. Hands drawn back, a crash helmet and a car's crumple zone all work this way. They cannot change the momentum that has to go, so they spread its removal over more time.

lead.text: The ball has to lose the same momentum whichever way it is caught. Only the time changes.

reveal.text: The same impulse of 20 N·s spread over 2 s needs 10 N.

lead.text: Stopping takes the cart's momentum down to zero over the time given.

reveal.text: The cart loses 24 kg·m/s over 3 s, an average force of −8 N.

lead.text: A ball that hits a wall and comes back changes more than it seems to. Take a 3 kg trolley moving right at 5 m/s that bounces off a spring and returns at 5 m/s to the left. Its speed is the same, so its kinetic energy is the same before and after: ½ × 3 × 5² = 37.5 J.

Its momentum is different. Before the bounce it is 3 × 5 = +15 kg·m/s. After it is 3 × (−5) = −15 kg·m/s. The change is −15 − 15 = −30 kg·m/s, so the spring gave the trolley an impulse of −30 N·s. That is twice the momentum the trolley started with, because the spring first had to remove the rightward momentum and then build the same amount in the other direction.
This is the difference between the two quantities. Kinetic energy follows only the speed, and momentum follows the velocity with its sign.
A 2 kg cart reverses from +4 m/s to −4 m/s.

reveal.text: Speed squared is the same, so kinetic energy is the same. Momentum changes by −16 kg·m/s.

lesson.orientation: Track signed momentum and use force acting over time to predict its change.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Throw a hard cricket ball to a friend and the catch stings. Throw the same ball so that your friend can draw their hands back as it lands, and the same catch is gentle. The ball arrives at the same speed both times and has to be brought to a stop both times, so the difference must lie in how the stop happens.

What differs is the time. Stiff hands stop the ball in a flash and hands that give way take longer. The sting is a force, and the force needed to stop a ball depends on how long you take over it. To put numbers on that, we need a way to say how much motion the ball carries and a way to say how a push changes it.
We follow one ball from the throw to the catch and put numbers on the sting.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find momentum and impulse, and use them to find a final velocity or an average force.

recap.keyIdea: Momentum is mass times velocity and carries a sign. Impulse, force times time, equals the change in momentum, so a longer stop needs a smaller force.

blocks.text: You found that stopping a ball over four times as long takes a quarter of the force. You also saw that a 2 kg cart reversing from +4 m/s to −4 m/s keeps its kinetic energy and flips its momentum.

recap.nextHook: When two carts collide, each pushes the other with the same force for the same time. Next we add up the momentum of both carts and see what the crash leaves unchanged.

questions.prompt: A 3 kg cart moves right at 4 m/s. With right positive, find its momentum in kg·m/s.
hints: Momentum is mass times signed velocity.
Use positive velocity for rightward motion.
Calculate 3 × 4.
questions.onCorrect: +12 kg·m/s. Momentum is mass times velocity, and rightward is positive.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the mass and the velocity. Momentum is their product.
The cart moves right, which is positive. So is its momentum.

questions.prompt: A constant net force of 6 N right acts for 3 s. With right positive, find the impulse in N·s.
hints: Impulse combines net force and its duration.
Multiply force by time.
Calculate 6 × 3.
questions.onCorrect: +18 N·s. Impulse is net force times the time it acts.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides force by time. Impulse is their product.
That adds force and time. Impulse is force times time.

questions.prompt: A 3 kg cart initially moves right at 4 m/s. A net impulse of +18 N·s acts. With right positive, find its final velocity in m/s.
hints: Find the initial momentum first.
Add the impulse to it.
Divide the new momentum by the mass.
questions.onCorrect: 10 m/s. Initial momentum plus impulse is final momentum; divide by mass for the velocity.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the impulse by the mass, which gives the change in velocity. Add the starting velocity.
That multiplies the final momentum by the mass. Divide by it instead.

questions.prompt: A cart reverses from +4 m/s to −4 m/s without changing mass. Which endpoint quantity is unchanged?
hints: Compare how velocity enters p = mv and K = ½mv².

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The speed squared is unchanged, so kinetic energy is the same; momentum and velocity reverse signs.

questions.onCorrect: Kinetic energy. Speed squared is the same either way, while velocity and momentum change sign.

misconceptions.feedback: Momentum carries the sign of the velocity, so it reverses.
The velocity goes from +4 to −4, so it is the thing that reverses.

questions.prompt: A 4 kg cart moving at +6 m/s stops in 3 s. Find the average net force in newtons with right positive.
hints: Stopping reduces the positive momentum to zero.
Divide the signed momentum change by time.
Divide the lost momentum by the stopping time and retain its negative sign.
questions.onCorrect: −8 N. The cart loses 24 kg·m/s over 3 s, so the average net force is negative.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but the force slows a rightward cart. It points left, so it is negative.
That multiplies by the time. Divide the momentum change by it.

questions.prompt: The same object undergoes the same momentum change over a longer stopping time. What happens to the magnitude of its average net force?
hints: Use F_avg = Δp/Δt with a fixed numerator.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The fixed impulse is spread over more time, reducing average force magnitude.

questions.onCorrect: It decreases. The same momentum change spread over more time needs a smaller average force.

misconceptions.feedback: Longer time in the denominator makes the force smaller, not larger.
The time is in the formula, so changing it changes the force.

questions.prompt: A ball is stopped by a steady 40 N force acting for 0.5 s. What steady force would stop the same ball over 2 s instead, in newtons?
hints: Is the job the same in both cases?
The same total push is needed, spread over more time.
The time is four times longer, so the force is a fraction of the first.
questions.onCorrect: 10 N. Force times time stays the same, so longer stopping time means a gentler force. That product is called impulse.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies by the extra time. A longer time needs a smaller force.
The same force for longer would stop more than the ball. A longer stop means less force.

questions.prompt: A 5 kg cart moves left at 2 m/s. With right positive, what is its momentum in kg·m/s?
hints: Momentum is mass times velocity.
Leftward velocity is negative.
Multiply the mass by the signed velocity.
questions.onCorrect: −10 kg·m/s. Momentum carries the sign of the velocity.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but the cart moves left. Momentum is negative.
That adds mass and velocity. Momentum is their product.

hints: Read each choice against the situation before you answer.

acceptedIdeas: Impulse is the change in momentum.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Impulse is the change in momentum.

choices.label: Impulse is the change in momentum.

questions.onCorrect: Final momentum is initial momentum plus the change, which is the impulse.

misconceptions.feedback: Impulse is in N·s, not m/s. It gives the change in momentum.
Impulse adds to momentum or takes from it depending on its sign. It does not always cancel.

questions.prompt: A 2 kg cart moves at +5 m/s. A net impulse of −6 N·s acts on it. What is its final velocity, in m/s?
hints: Find the initial momentum first.
Add the impulse, with its sign.
Divide the final momentum by the mass.
questions.onCorrect: 2 m/s. A negative impulse takes momentum away, so the cart slows.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the impulse instead of subtracting it. Its sign is negative.
That divides the impulse alone by the mass. Add it to the initial momentum first.

The ball starts moving right and ends at rest.
Divide the momentum change by the time.
questions.onCorrect: −20 N. The force acts against the motion, so it is negative.
